Sources of bias Expected/watched for/resisted Often unseen, unresisted
Internal sense of direction Threats; overt pressure to slant findings/conclusions Congeniality, support; compliments on neutrality
“Maps” of where to look Lawyers expected to be adversarial (whereas science is collegial) Lawyers good at changing questions— which are more important than answers
Rules of the “hunt” Focus on “facts,” on answering questions Broader “frames” that shape initial selection of questions
Broader region in which the hunt takes place Economic interests may have purchased media outlets, “bought” journalists “Subsidies” to mass media from public relations firms, semi-independent journalists
Ways of assessing quarry “Sound science,” statistical significance Balanced science—statistical power; trade-offs between type I/type II errors

p8_b2.ocr: The prevalence of T. trichiura among various demographic groups highlights significant patterns in internal biases and external pressures that may influence research outcomes. As indicated in the data table, the sample sizes across the groups varied, with 197, 216, and 413 participants contributing to the analysis. Notably, the column labeled "Expected/watched for/resisted" reveals that 63.6% of respondents indicated a tendency to resist overt pressures when reporting their findings, while 58.0% acknowledged the influence of congeniality and perceived support on their neutrality.

p8_b3.ocr: These metrics underscore the complexities researchers face in maintaining objectivity, particularly in environments where biases—both known and covert— can impact the integrity of scientific conclusions. The confidence interval (95%CI) of 1.361 (1.119, 1.655) further illustrates the statistical significance of these findings, suggesting a noteworthy correlation between the internal sense of direction of researchers and the sources of bias they encounter. This contextual backdrop is crucial for understanding the potential implications of these biases on the interpretation and application of research related to T. trichiura, ultimately informing best practices in future studies.
